subtype: Approach: trying to time the market [Pitfall]
passage:
Mentor's note, June. Varun writing about Binita, a colleague I have coached this year.
March: prices fell, and Binita paused the monthly plan, saying "I'll restart at the very bottom." April: prices rose a little. "It's a trap, another dip is coming," Binita said. May: higher again, and Binita kept the same line, checking the numbers every evening.
June: prices are well above where the plan was paused. Binita sounded tense and said, "If I buy now I'll feel stupid, and if I don't I'll feel stupid."
I am not an adviser, so I only asked what price would count as the bottom. Binita could not name one. We agreed to talk again next week.
— Varun

qa.q: When did Binita pause the monthly plan?
qa.a: Binita paused the monthly plan in March.

qa.q: What was Binita feeling in June?
qa.a: Binita was tense and torn, saying that either choice would feel stupid.

qa.q: What could Binita try instead of waiting for a lower price?
qa.a: Binita could restart a fixed monthly amount on a set date, which does not need a guess at the bottom, and check with a registered adviser if unsure.

qa.q: What is it like for Varun to watch Binita's waiting?
qa.a: Varun feels concerned but careful, since Varun is not an adviser and can only ask questions and stay in touch.

grounding: The note shows an investor who stops a monthly plan to wait for the bottom and keeps waiting for a lower price after the market rebounds.

passage:
January, a quiet Sunday. Ira wrote a rule on an index card: "If shares fall so that they are much less of my mix, move a small slice from the steady holdings into shares." She stuck it inside the notebook.
March, the week of the crash. Ira's shares had dropped and the mix had drifted. Lokesh, her friend, texted, "You're not actually buying more now, are you?" Ira read the card twice. "I wrote this when I was calm," she replied. Her hands were cold as she moved the slice.
April. Prices were still unsteady, but the mix was back near the plan. Ira added a line to the card: "Review once a year." Lokesh sent a thumbs-up.

qa.q: Where did Ira keep the rule?
qa.a: Ira kept the rule inside the notebook.

qa.q: What was Ira feeling when moving the slice in March?
qa.a: Ira was nervous, shown by the cold hands, but held to the card because she wrote it while calm.

qa.q: What could Ira do if she started to doubt the rule during a fall?
qa.a: Ira could talk it over with a registered adviser before changing the card, rather than changing it in the heat of the moment.

qa.q: How might Lokesh have felt seeing Ira follow the card?
qa.a: Lokesh was worried at first, given the sharp text, and later relieved enough to send a thumbs-up.

grounding: The passage shows an investor following a rule written in a calm period by moving a small share into equity when the mix drifts.

subtype: Approach: limiting news and checking on a schedule [Thinking]
passage:
Come, Deepak, sit down and put that phone face down. I'm Ankita, and I'll tell you how I stopped doing what you're doing.
A few years ago, when prices were falling, I checked them at breakfast, at lunch and again at night. My stomach was in knots by evening, and I kept wanting to sell just to make it stop. My flatmate Meghna said, "You've been snapping at everyone."
That was the moment I saw it: the more I looked, the more I panicked. So I muted every market channel and picked one day a month, the first Sunday, to open the portfolio for half an hour.
The urge to act didn't vanish. But by the first Sunday it was smaller.

qa.q: Which day of the month did Ankita choose to look at the portfolio?
qa.a: Ankita chose the first Sunday of the month.

qa.q: What was Ankita feeling in the evenings when prices were falling?
qa.a: Ankita was anxious, with a knotted stomach and an urge to sell just to make it stop.

qa.q: Ankita muted market channels and chose one day a month. What did that choice help with?
qa.a: It reduced constant checking, which was feeding the panic, so the urge to act on impulse grew smaller.

qa.q: How did Meghna see Ankita's habit of checking prices?
qa.a: Meghna saw a flatmate who had become sharp and irritable with everyone, which is why Meghna said so out loud.

grounding: The elder's story shows an investor who notices that constant price checking raises anxiety and checks once a month while muting market channels.

subtype: Approach: following a friend's tip on a hot stock [Pitfall]
passage:
Monday
Charu: Have you seen that stock? It's beaten down. It'll double, I'm sure of it.
Payal: How sure?
Charu: Very. Someone at lunch said so. Don't wait too long.

Payal: The stock is down again. Just read the annual report. It has huge debts, and interest payments eat everything.
Charu: Oh no. I only heard it from someone else. I'm so sorry 😢
Payal: I'm not blaming you. I should have looked before.
Charu: What will you do now?
Payal: Read properly. And talk to someone qualified before I put anything else in.

qa.a: Charu felt guilty and embarrassed about passing on a tip heard second-hand, as the sorry message shows.

subtype: Approach: learning from a past drawdown [Revision]
passage:
The deadline to change the fund mix was three o'clock, and Sudha had two hours and a slow internet line. Yogesh, at the next desk, leaned across. "Did you sell?"
"No." Sudha pulled out a notebook from two years back, the pages soft at the corners. Last time a smaller fall had scared her, and she had waited, and it had come back within months. But her own note said something else too: "Too much in one risky sector. I felt sick every day."
"So you're doing nothing again?"
"Nothing except this." Sudha moved a small part out of that sector before the window closed and kept the rest as planned.
Then Sudha closed the laptop and took a breath.

qa.q: What time was the deadline to change the fund mix?
qa.a: The deadline was three o'clock.

qa.q: What was Sudha feeling in the notebook entry from two years ago?
qa.a: Sudha felt sick and scared about the risky sector, as the note itself says.

qa.q: What could Sudha do if the risky sector recovers before the next review?
qa.a: Sudha could leave the smaller share as it is and review it at the planned time, not chase the recovery.

qa.q: How might Yogesh have seen Sudha's choice?
qa.a: Yogesh seemed unsure, asking if Sudha was doing nothing again, though the small move shows a plan behind the calm.

grounding: The passage shows an investor who recalls a smaller earlier fall that recovered, reads past notes and sticks with the plan while lowering exposure to one risky sector.

subtype: Approach: talking to a registered adviser [Action]
passage:
Thursday, evening.
Went to see Gurleen today, a registered adviser who charges a fee only, no commission. I was nervous and had a page of questions.
Gurleen said at the start she couldn't tell me what to do with my money. What she could do was explain how general options work: how the time I need the money changes what makes sense, what fees do over the years, and what "rebalancing" means. I wrote it all down.
It was an odd feeling: less like getting orders, more like being taught.
I'll go through the notes on my own this week and decide after that. I'm calmer than I was this morning.
— Parveen

qa.q: Who did Parveen go to see?
qa.a: Parveen went to see Gurleen.

qa.q: How did Parveen feel about the meeting by the evening?
qa.a: Parveen was calmer, having been nervous that morning, and liked feeling taught instead of ordered.

qa.q: What could Parveen do with the notes from the meeting?
qa.a: Parveen could go through them slowly, mark the parts that are unclear and take those questions back to Gurleen.

qa.q: How might Gurleen see the purpose of the meeting?
qa.a: Gurleen sees it as explaining how general options work, and said so at the start, leaving the decision to Parveen.

grounding: The diary shows a person unsure about a portfolio mix who meets a registered adviser paid by fee only, treating the talk as learning rather than an instruction.

subtopic: Building insurance and an emergency fund
subtype: Approach: sizing the fund from fixed monthly costs [Thinking]
passage:
On the crowded bus home, Manoj had four minutes of phone battery and a receipt in his pocket. Kamal, a friend from the office, squeezed in beside him.
"What are you writing?" Kamal asked.
"Sums for an emergency fund. Rent, fifteen thousand. Food, eight. The loan instalment, six. What I send home, five." Manoj added it: thirty-four thousand. "If I lost my job, that's what I'd need every month. Times six, so two lakh and four thousand."
"That's a lot."
"It's a target, though. I'll build it over two years. That comes to eight thousand five hundred a month."
Manoj circled the number. It felt smaller once it was on paper.

qa.q: How much did Manoj add up for the monthly costs?
qa.a: Manoj added up thirty-four thousand.

qa.q: What was Manoj feeling as he circled the number?
qa.a: Manoj felt some relief, because the number felt smaller once it was on paper.

qa.q: What could Manoj do if eight thousand five hundred a month is too much?
qa.a: Manoj could stretch the time to more than two years or start with a smaller monthly sum and increase it later.

qa.q: How might Kamal have seen Manoj's sums on the receipt?
qa.a: Kamal may have felt surprised at the size of the target, saying it was a lot, but curious enough to keep listening.

grounding: The passage shows a person totalling rent, food, loan payments and family support, multiplying by six for the target and dividing it into a monthly saving goal.

passage:
"I keep saying I'll save what's left at the end of the month," Rehana said at the bank counter. "There's never anything left."
"Then let's not leave it to the end," Vinita said. "On the day your salary arrives, the bank can shift a set sum into a different savings account by itself. You won't need to remember."
"How much do I set?"
"An amount that doesn't hurt. Five thousand?"
Rehana hesitated, then nodded. "And I can change it later?"
"Any time."
Rehana signed the form. Two months later she came back to the same counter.
"It moved on the first, both times," she said. "I didn't even feel it."
Vinita smiled. "That's the point."

qa.q: What does the standing instruction move on salary day?
qa.a: It moves a set sum into a different savings account.

qa.q: What was Rehana feeling while signing the form?
qa.a: Rehana was hesitant but hopeful, shown by the pause, the question about changing it later and the nod.

qa.q: What could Rehana do once the amount feels easy?
qa.a: Rehana could raise the amount a little, keeping the same automatic transfer so no willpower is needed.

qa.q: How might Vinita see the standing instruction?
qa.a: Vinita sees it as a simple tool that removes the need to remember, and smiles when Rehana says the transfer did not hurt.

grounding: The dialogue shows a standing instruction moving a set sum into another account on salary day, so saving needs no willpower each month.

subtopic: Building insurance and an emergency fund
passage:
Friday night.
Every time Kishore asked if I'd started saving, I said, "After the next raise." Kishore asked twice this year, and I laughed both times.
Then the raises came. And the rent went up, I upgraded my phone, and dinners out became a weekly thing. The money vanished quietly, as always.
Today I woke in the night with a sharp pain and Kishore took me to the hospital. It was a short stay. The bill came before I'd left, and I had nothing put away. Kishore paid the difference without saying a word.
I'm glad I'm okay. I'm ashamed I had no plan. Tomorrow I'll write down what I earn, and what I spend.
— Keerthana

qa.q: How many times did Kishore ask about saving this year?
qa.a: Kishore asked twice this year.

qa.q: How does Keerthana feel about having no plan?
qa.a: Keerthana is ashamed, as the entry says, although also grateful and relieved that Keerthana is okay.

qa.q: What could Keerthana do first now that the bill is paid?
qa.a: Keerthana could start with a small fixed amount each month right away, and repay Kishore on a plan.

qa.q: How might Kishore have felt paying the difference?
qa.a: Kishore was probably worried and a little frustrated but chose to help quietly, since Kishore did not say a word.

grounding: The diary shows a person who keeps postponing saving until a raise while expenses rise, and a hospital bill arrives before any reserve exists.

Minakshi, put the kettle on and sit. You're about to choose a health policy, so let me tell you how I did it. I'm Trisha.
The agent who phoned me was smooth. "Just sign today, it's the best." I said no and took the brochures home.
I made a table. Down one side, several insurers; across, the things that matter: how much cover, how long before certain things are covered, the limit on room rent, what is left out, and how often the company actually settles claims. Then I read the small print, line by line, with a pencil.
Two policies that looked alike turned out very different on room rent and exclusions. That saved me from a nasty surprise.
The agent called back twice. I just said I'd decided.

qa.q: How many times did the agent call back?
qa.a: The agent called back twice.

qa.q: What was Trisha probably feeling when the agent said "Just sign today"?
qa.a: Trisha was probably wary and unhurried, since Trisha said no and took the brochures home.

qa.q: Trisha chose to make a table and read the small print. What did that choice help with?
qa.a: It showed how two similar-looking policies differed on room rent and exclusions, so Trisha avoided a nasty surprise.

qa.q: How might the agent have seen Trisha's refusal to sign on the spot?
qa.a: The agent probably saw a customer who would not be rushed, which is why the agent called back twice.

grounding: The elder's story shows a person comparing health policies on a checklist of cover, waiting periods, room rent limits, exclusions and claim record, and reading the small print.
